Jan Zelivsky
yan zhe'liv-skee
n. (Jan Zelivsky, died 1422, radical preacher of Prague at St Mary of the Snows, who led the crowd of the first defenestration)
Zelivsky, Czech, of Zeliv, the Premonstratensian house where he had been a canon; Jan, the Czech form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jan Zelivsky was a former canon of Zeliv who became preacher at the church of St Mary of the Snows in the New Town of Prague, and for three years the most powerful man in the city. He preached daily to the artisans and the poor, in Czech, on the Apocalypse and the prophets, with the cup administered to all and the whole programme of the Four Articles pressed as a demand upon the magistrates. On the thirtieth of July 1419 he led a procession from his church to the New Town hall to require the release of imprisoned Hussites; the crowd forced the building, and the councillors were thrown from the windows to the pikes below. That act began the Hussite wars. For the next three years Zelivsky governed Prague through the assembly of the commons, appointed and removed its officers, and was accused by his enemies of doing by tumult what he could not carry by argument. The patrician party took him by a stratagem in March 1422 and beheaded him in the Old Town hall. The dictionary enters him as a necessary warning, because he is on the right side of the doctrinal question and on the wrong side of the means: a preacher of the word of God who built a political power on his own congregation and used a crowd as an instrument.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a tumult as the commotion of a multitude; sedition as a factious commotion of the people; and zeal as passionate ardor in the pursuit of any object.

expand to see more

TUMULT, n. [L. tumultus.] The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion.

SEDITION, n. [L. seditio.] A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.

ZEAL, n. [Gr. to boil.] Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this ardor in human beings is a mixture of good and evil affections.

MULTITUDE, n. [L. multitudo.] A great number, indefinitely; a crowd or throng; the populace.

MAGISTRACY, n. The office or dignity of a magistrate; the body of magistrates.

Modern Corruption

Prague radical preacher who led the crowd of the first defenestration in 1419, governed the city by its commons for three years, and was beheaded in 1422.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the preacher who makes his pulpit a political engine and his congregation a crowd. Zelivsky's doctrine of the cup was right and his demand that public sin be punished was in the Four Articles; the means by which he pressed both was a mob at a town hall, and men were killed by it. “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) was fulfilled upon him within three years, by the same city. The dictionary does not treat this as an excess to be excused by the provocation. It treats it as the thing itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the preached word as the preacher's weapon. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole of the commission, and it is enough; it converted the Roman empire without a riot. A minister who concludes that the word is too slow and reaches for the crowd has stopped believing the doctrine he preaches about the power of the word, whatever he says in the pulpit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek machaira (G3162), a sword; Greek exousia (G1849), authority, delegated power.

expand to see more

Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword, a short blade; “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword”, Matthew 26:52.

Greek topos (G5117) — a place; “Put up again thy sword into his place”, Matthew 26:52.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Greek ekdikos (G1558) — an avenger; “a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil”, Romans 13:4.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word”, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Usage

"“Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52) — the procession to the New Town hall, the thirtieth of July 1419."

"“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — three years of government by the assembly of the commons."

"“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — the commission that is enough, and that he judged too slow."
